title: How Will You Know When Manufacturing’s AI Revolution Arrives? You May Not.
text:
Want to experience the power of AI? Go prompt a generative AI engine to write you an email, build you a PowerPoint, or create imagery from scratch.
Want to experience the power of AI within manufacturing? That’s going to be a little trickier.
After all, there are only so many back-office jobs within this industry that require the sort of creativity and content production that has given ChatGPT and others its notoriety.
That doesn’t mean manufacturing isn’t set to benefit from artificial intelligence. AI is already having a tremendous impact on manufacturers across the U.S., and most analyses put it among the industries that will experience the most benefit from AI.
Hard to imagine, considering what so many of us think of when we hear the phrase artificial intelligence. But in fact, AI is already very much a part of manufacturing and will only become more entwined in the near future. Let’s dive into how.
AI In Robots, ERP, And Beyond
Here’s the truth: The age of AI in manufacturing is already here, even if many manufacturing employees haven’t noticed much change. That’s because the technology will mostly be introduced to manufacturers via the technology they already have in place.
Take a standard enterprise resource planning system, for example. ERP providers are rapidly installing AI into their systems. They’re introducing AI tools that help streamline the sales process and provide deeper customer analytics and insights. Some use cases are industry-specific, built as solutions to specific problems. Others are as simple as introducing AI assistants and chat tools that help users rapidly query a wide range of data and find the information they’re looking for.
And then there are collaborative robots, that form of robotic automation that works hand-in-hand with humans along an assembly line. Human-created algorithms provide the foundation for these machines, but increasingly, developers are finding ways to improve their productivity through AI. That means allowing an AI engine to observe a cobot’s actions, learn how it works, and suggest tweaks to the machine’s processes that may improve the manufacturer’s operation.
For that matter, there are many optimization tasks where empirical learning by a computer will lead to better processes than what humans can pull off today without AI. Computers are much more adept at measuring the last 1,000 or 1 million times something has been done and understanding what went wrong, what went right, and how things could be improved going forward.
Eventually, that continuous optimization loop will take place without human intervention. Cobots on our manufacturing floors will pick up on things and modify their behavior to be more efficient without human engineers stepping in to reprogram.
AI, too, will get better and better at telling us when a machine does require human involvement. Fueled by sensors feeding information to an AI engine, predictive maintenance will allow our companies to pinpoint upcoming maintenance needs before they occur, thereby decreasing machine downtime and saving money.
Beyond creating efficiencies, there’s a more global upside that AI in manufacturing presents. Our systems will be better equipped to interact with the systems of vendors and other companies, understand the availability and timing of certain materials, and provide clearer timelines. Over time, we’ll be able to more accurately forecast how long it takes to create certain products and get them out the door to customers or to the next vendor along the supply chain. We’ll improve the way we think about supply and demand. And it will all feed into a more powerful, efficient, and resilient supply chain.
Manufacturers Can Likely Use AI More Than They Are
All that said, there are ways manufacturers can take a more intentional approach to using AI today. It’s likely that most manufacturers have not fully explored the technology.
ChatGPT can help companies create marketing copy, blog posts, emails, and white paper drafts with much greater efficiency. It can also help find suppliers—Gen AI trained on the entire internet will be able to easily locate information that a simple Google search won’t quickly produce. Some companies have begun experimenting with ChatGPT to write code, while others are using it to speed up the process of formulating contracts and completing other tedious paperwork.
A major hurdle for the technology, of course, is cybersecurity. Anything entered into ChatGPT could theoretically make its way into the public, of particular concern for sensitive data like vendor contracts. Over time, we’ll overcome those hurdles, and AI will make manufacturers’ lives easier. Of course, it won’t revolutionize the industry—only bring incremental improvement.
AI Won’t Fundamentally Reshape Manufacturing—But It Will Enable Future Innovation
Over the next decade, AI will be doing everything from creating dynamic content to driving cars to, very likely, assisting medical diagnoses. On its face, it may be difficult to grasp how our industry stands to benefit as much as some of the others. Contrary to what will happen in some other industries, AI won’t fundamentally reshape manufacturing.
Instead, it will make so much of what we already do better. Our cobots will self-optimize. Our machines will alert us when they require maintenance. Our ERP systems will be well-oiled machines, connected and communicating with others to optimize timing and production. And, yes, our back offices and development teams will be enhanced through the magic of AI-powered content creation.
That will all have the effect of creating an industry prepared to innovate. We already know that the U.S. won’t be able to compete on certain products with countries where labor costs are low. Our goal is not to retake everything we outsourced to China over the last 20 years. But it should be to lead the world in manufacturing innovation, so that, through technology, companies here are able to do more with less and become more competitive. With AI, that future is there for the taking.

title: 5 Retail Trends Steering Product Content Journeys
text:
Data is – and always will be – the most important asset for any company. It's what powers their entire operation. In retail, the data that drives product content is what makes a business come alive. It’s how retailers make their products discoverable, enticing, and purchasable.
However, the road to delivering perfect product content to consumers is constantly changing, making it crucial for every retailer to adapt to evolving trends. In analyzing today’s intersection of technology and consumer behavior, we’re seeing five key trends steering product content journeys: personalization, omnichannel strategies, returns management, consumer engagement, and AI integration.
1. Selling on social
We attend concerts on TikTok, play games on LinkedIn, and of course – buy our favorite products on Facebook. According to a recent Prosper Insights & Analytics survey, nearly 30% of Millennials said they use the "shop now" feature on Facebook to buy products regularly.
“As we spend more and more time on social media, it only makes sense retailers are increasingly looking to these platforms as grounds for shopping experiences,” says Katie Moro, Global Director of Managed Service at Productsup, a Product-to-Consumer (P2C) software company. “We’re seeing product content for social commerce evolve in several key ways.” Those include:
Personalization: Leveraging user data and AI algorithms, social commerce can deliver highly personalized shopping experiences. This personalization enables retailers to target users with tailored product recommendations based on their interests, browsing history, and social interactions.
Augmented reality: AR technology allows users to virtually try on products such as clothing, makeup, and accessories before making a purchase. Providing this level of product information through immersive shopping experiences boosts confidence in online purchases by reducing uncertainty.
Streamlined purchasing: Shoppers no longer have to deal with the inconvenience of being redirected to another site to purchase a product they stumbled upon on social. Native checkout on platforms like TikTok Shop makes transactions frictionless, leading to higher conversion rates for retailers. In fact, TikTok users are 1.2 times more likely to buy from the same retailer again when TikTok is part of the purchase journey.
2. Offering omnichannel
“There was a point in time when we all thought we’d bid farewell to brick-and-mortar for good. While the world is becoming more digital, ecommerce will never make physical shopping obsolete,” says Moro. Instead, Moro goes on to say that creating blended experiences through omnichannel retail has become essential to staying competitive. Retailers need to keep the following factors in mind when delivering “phygital” product content:
Digital integration: As brick-and-mortar stores bring digital touchpoints into their stores, such as offering mobile apps for in-store navigation and digital signage for personalized recommendations, they need to ensure product content is consistent in both mediums. If an item says “in-stock” on a mobile app but is discovered to be unavailable in-store, shoppers become discouraged from trusting these omnichannel experiences.
Store-within-stores: Collaborations between retailers to create "store-within-a-store" concepts continue to grow, such as Target and Kendra Scott, allowing brands to reach new audiences and offer customers a curated selection of complementary products or services in one convenient location. This model requires product content to be stored in a way that makes sharing data between retailers and brands easy.
3. Reducing returns
One of the biggest challenges retailers face today is managing returns. Taking more control over the path product content takes as it moves between suppliers and buyers can make a significant impact on reducing the number of times shoppers send back items. How? According to Moro, retailers are increasingly turning to the following return strategies:
Streamlined returns: Retailers are investing in automation to streamline the return process, offering options such as online return portals, QR code-based returns, or self-service kiosks in-store to expedite returns and reduce wait times.
Improved quality: By improving product content quality and providing accurate product descriptions, retailers can reduce the likelihood of returns due to dissatisfaction or misrepresentation. Enhanced product images, detailed sizing information, and customer reviews can help set realistic expectations and reduce the incidence of returns.
Preventative measurements: Retailers are implementing proactive measures to prevent unnecessary returns, such as offering virtual fit guides, size recommendation tools, or personalized product recommendations based on past purchases and preferences. By helping customers make more informed purchasing decisions upfront, retailers can reduce the need for returns later on.
4. Competing for consumer spend
While the economy is slowly recovering, consumer spending is still tight. To distinguish themselves from competitors and create a frictionless shopping experience that builds brand loyalty, retailers need to be strategic in how they manage their product content:
Personalized targeting: Data analytics and AI-driven insights enable retailers to create personalized messaging and offers based on consumer preferences, behaviors, and demographics.
Increased transparency: Building trust and transparency with consumers is absolutely crucial. Retailers should add more details to product content, such as product attributes, sourcing practices, and sustainability efforts, as well as ensure all information is accurate and up to date. Eventually, disclosing certain product data will become mandated through initiatives like digital product passports.
Agile processes: As trends come and go week by week, retailers need to have the flexibility and adaptability to adjust campaigns in real time. Product content requires agility in adjusting inventory levels, diversifying product offerings, optimizing supply chain processes, and exploring new distribution channels to stay competitive.
5. Advancing with AI
And of course, the biggest disruptor of retail operations – AI. But how is AI impacting product content journeys specifically?
Personalization: AI algorithms can deliver personalized product recommendations based on factors such as past purchase history, browsing behavior, demographic information, and contextual data. The advancement of generative AI also makes it easy for retailers to tailor messaging and visuals for ads and listings based on distinct demographics and regions.
Dynamic pricing optimization: AI can enable dynamic pricing optimization, allowing retailers to adjust prices in real time based on factors like demand, competition, and inventory levels. This dynamic pricing strategy can help retailers maximize revenue, optimize margins, and remain competitive in a rapidly changing market landscape.
Data capture: Looking at backend retail processes, AI provides tremendous efficiency in sourcing product content and converting it to required formats. For instance, optical character recognition and AI can be combined to extract product data from labels, removing manual processes that slow down time-to-market and leave room for human error.
By embracing these trends and continually adapting their product content journeys, retailers can set themselves up for long-term commerce success. “The key lies in understanding and anticipating consumer needs, harnessing the power of technology to enhance experiences, and fostering transparency and trust in every interaction,” states Moro.

title: Generative AI: To Generate Real Value, Adapt The Organization
text:
It’s the organizational question that has been top of mind for executives for nearly a year now: How do I change my operating model to quickly generate value and results from generative AI?
The wealth of possibilities—and their organizational implications—can be overwhelming. By 2026, more than 80% of enterprises will have used generative AI application programming interfaces or deployed generative AI-enabled applications, according to Gartner.
However, there’s a difference between pockets of experimentation and a scalable, organization-wide approach that achieves tangible results. To bridge the gap, it’s important for executives to first distinguish between two types of value: 1) new businesses or changes to the customer offering, and 2) operational changes to support the existing business.
Building Businesses With Generative AI
The biggest potential sources of value lie in building new businesses and evolving the customer offering. From an operating model standpoint, this often requires dedicated, multi-disciplinary teams with enough distance from the core business and a clear sandbox where they can break rules and move fast.
In some instances, this may also require a more formal, executive-led program where decisions can be escalated and resolved quickly. Companies in highly regulated industries, such as financial services, understandably tend to shy away from the “break rules” part, opting instead for greater oversight on new businesses that hold promise. One leading global financial services company, for example, has launched an executive-sponsored approach of this kind.
Scaling a new customer use case can involve small contributions from hundreds of people. Accomplishing that kind of re-prioritization and alignment quickly can only be done with top-down sponsorship. Such sponsorship from the CEO allowed grocer Carrefour to launch Hopla, its customer assistant, in about six weeks.
Augmenting Work With Generative AI
However, most of the discussion around generative AI today is not about building new businesses or customer offerings, but about how the technology will change existing operations and reshape the workforce. Far from a doomsday scenario of a jobless future, only 4 of 27 industries expect net job losses as a result of AI, according to an August 2023 World Economic Forum study. Respondents surveyed for that study believe only an additional 9% of operational tasks will be automated in the next five years, supporting the idea that AI is more likely to augment jobs than replace them. Other predictive studies on potential augmentation or labor time saved from generative AI range from 12% to 34%. At Bain & Company, we estimate 20%, based on an assessment of 14 sample companies across industries.
Of course, the actual effect will be felt unevenly across capabilities and roles. In our experience at Bain, some use cases show results in line with averages. At one energy company, an AI assistant to support service agents was able to reduce customer handling time by 17%. Other use cases far exceed the averages. For example, my colleagues found that AI reduced the time needed to generate initial regulatory filing drafts at a healthcare company by around 73% when accounting for review and quality control, turning a multi-month endeavor into a weeks-long task.
Generative AI provides an opportunity for companies to make jobs better by eliminating undesirable work and creating more joyful routines. Done right, becoming more digital should always mean becoming more human.
So, how can organizations evolve to capture the most value? Adapting the operating model for work augmented by generative AI is similar to any other technology adoption. Changing the work means editing job descriptions, supporting skill development for new tools, and redesigning processes. Take an entry-level job, say, a junior engineer—the engineer is still accountable for creating code that performs as intended, but the day-to-day role may become more about code review and synthesis than code development. That frees up more time for the engineer to explore customer experience improvements or groundbreaking product features.
Similarly, team size is unlikely to change dramatically because it is defined by the nature of the work. Engineering teams likely will still function best with around six to eight people. Even if AI can handle more routine customer calls, call centers may still run teams of 15 because the higher value calls that remain are more complex and take longer, requiring a human touch.
Process redesign is often overlooked or undervalued in technology adoption because of limited collaboration between the business and technology teams. It’s imperative to have close partnership across technology, data science, and business teams to remove friction and make it easier to change the way work is done.
While many companies have engaged in isolated pilots and scattered experimentation, few have progressed to a structured, scalable enterprise-wide approach that delivers real value. In the next stage of adoption, the ability to adapt the operating model for generative AI will separate the best from the rest. Some organizations are uniquely advantaged. Their operating models already embrace change, and they are used to standing up or standing down teams around new opportunities and priorities. These leaders are moving fast with generative AI—and the results are starting to show.

title: Council Post: 15 Offbeat Interview Questions Candidates Should Prepare To Answer
text:
For job applicants, the interview process offers a vital opportunity to showcase their professional skills and suitability for a company. As such, candidates should put their best foot forward by preparing for potential interview questions.
While most job seekers have a prepared answer for standard or commonly asked questions, they may need clarification when presented with more offbeat lines of questioning. To help, the members of Forbes Human Resources Council share some unique interview questions that could come up and why it's important to have a solid response ready.
1. 'How do you de-stress?'
“What do you do to manage stress or de-stress?” There's no wrong or right answer, but it allows an opportunity for candidates to share what activities they enjoy, and also to incorporate the importance of well-being. This has been a top priority for organizations these past four years and will continue to be included as a benefit in future-forward organizations. - Teedra Bernard, TransUnion
2. 'What gives you energy?'
I ask candidates, "What gives you energy and what drains you in your current role?" The answer gives me insight into the tasks or goals of their current job they enjoy, or have an affinity for, as well as reveals their least favorite tasks or job responsibilities. If their "drainers" make up more than 25% of the job I am considering them for, they probably are not a good fit for the role. - Anne McCafferty, Hale Trailer, Brake & Wheel
3. 'When did you last acquire a new skill?'
"Tell me about the last time you acquired a new skill and how you applied it." With nearly 25% of jobs being set to be disrupted in the next five years, according to the World Economic Forum's latest "Future of Jobs" report, learning agility, the motivation and method to acquire new skills at pace is critical to maintaining relevance and increasing employability. - Catalina Schveninger, Matara Consulting
4. 'How has a setback shaped your growth?'
"Can you share an example of a challenging experience or setback you've faced and how it shaped your professional growth?" It seems like a standard interview question, but it's important because it focuses on assessing qualities like resilience, grit and a growth mindset over technical skills, and allows employers to gauge how candidates handle adversity and learn from it. - Tia Smith, Cognizant
5. 'What did you learn from failure?'
"Talk to me about a time you have failed. What did you learn from it?" With the rise of AI and technology across all fields, organizations are looking for individuals willing to innovate and learn. With trying new things, ideas and technologies, the chance of failure also exists. Companies are looking for individuals willing to learn, fail, innovate and succeed. - Amee Parekh, Stello Technologies
Forbes Human Resources Council is an invitation-only organization for HR executives across all industries. Do I qualify?
6. 'How do you learn new systems?'
"What systems and/or technology have you used, and what's one thing you do to hold yourself accountable to learning a new system? Please provide an example." As technology evolves and alternative technologies emerge, it's important that candidates not only have experience using multiple systems but that they've had to learn and adapt to new systems within an existing organization. - Jenna Hinrichsen, Advanced RPO
7. 'Are you willing to work in person?'
One question every candidate should be ready to answer, especially for a remote job, is, "Would you be willing to shift to an on-site or hybrid role if your employer required you to do so?” This question establishes expectations upfront for possible location-related situations and is a timely topic being addressed in the hiring and recruitment industries right now, with varying opinions. - Laura Spawn, Virtual Vocations, Inc.
8. 'What don't you want here?'
Candidates are also screening us, so a good question is, "What is something that you wouldn't like to find here?" Not only will you know if they heard what you were saying or if they researched about your company, but you also could understand what the person values the most (leadership, communication, benefits, training, development and so on). You can know if it's a proper fit. - Marcela Pizzi, Atlas Renewable Energy
9. 'How are you using AI currently?'
"How are you using AI?" Being ready to discuss your experience and views on AI signals that you're knowledgeable about this emerging field and its impacts on the future of work. It also shows your technology fluency and that you can apply AI to solve problems and increase productivity. This "AI readiness" question cuts to the chase in assessing a candidate's technology IQ and literacy. - Nicole Smartt Serres, Smartt Enterprises
10. 'How would you use AI in this role?'
"How would you use AI to bring more efficiency to this job?" This question would get both at how deeply the candidate understands the role and responsibilities and also how familiar they are with the uses of AI to be able to think about some practical ways they could apply it for their job. - Sanja Licina, QuestionPro
11. 'How do you handle ambiguity?'
“How do you handle ambiguity?” Change is a cornerstone of the 2024 job market, so find out how candidates will complete tasks, even with limited information or experience. Do they struggle to deal with change or can they pivot as new challenges arise? Adaptability is an essential soft skill. - Ursula Mead, InHerSight
12. 'What concerns did you have about the job?'
"What specific concern (from research) gave you pause about our company, and how did you overcome it?" The benefits: 1. It's engaging and introspective, and prompts reflection and honest dialogue, 2. It uncovers potential concerns and shows the candidate's ability to research and address them, 3. It gauges resilience and problem-solving and demonstrates the ability to overcome doubts. - Michael D. Brown, Global Recruiters of Buckhead
13. 'How do you fit into our culture?'
“How do you see yourself fitting into our organizational culture?” Recruiters are increasingly recognizing the importance of hiring candidates who align with their employer’s mission, values and culture. Any job candidate should be prepared to talk about how they would fit into the organization’s culture and how they would contribute. - Niki Jorgensen, Insperity
14. 'How do you start your day?'
One question that I've heard hiring managers use is "Tell me about how you start your day." It can catch candidates off guard. What they are looking for is whether you are intentional and structured about your time. Talking about spending time planning your day, listening to educational podcasts, reading, meditating, exercising and so on are all great responses and tell a lot about a person. - Hazel Kassu, Sudduth Search
15. 'How did you adapt to tech evolution?'
"How did you adapt to a rapidly evolving technology environment?" The question probes the candidate's adaptability, learning agility and innovation skills. - Britton Bloch, Navy Federal

title: 4 Steps To Becoming AI Ready With Microsoft Copilot
text:
“With great power comes great responsibility.” Although Uncle Ben originally imparted this wisdom to Spider-Man, there isn’t a more important guiding principle for business leaders to follow when becoming AI ready.
In early 2024, Microsoft made Copilot for Microsoft 365, its AI assistant, widely available to organizations of all sizes. This represents a huge opportunity for companies to take advantage of the powerful productivity gains possible with AI.
But there’s also big potential risk around compliance, data privacy and job disruption. Careful, intentional preparation is necessary both to ensure successful adoption and to mitigate the risks associated with artificial intelligence.
Why You Shouldn’t Wait To Get Ready For Copilot
Microsoft Copilot can accomplish an impressive array of tasks, including instantly summarizing large bodies of content; retrieving and synthesizing information saved across multiple files; analyzing data; and drafting emails, articles and presentations.
Early adopter results speak to the impact this tool can have. According to Microsoft, 70% of users said Copilot made them more productive, 57% said it made them more creative and 68% said it improved their work quality.
In other words, Copilot has the potential to transform work. Organizations that become AI ready now will quickly realize productivity gains, leaving their competitors behind. Think of it like compound interest. Copilot and similar AI tools learn and improve as they’re used, so investing now not only means value today but increasing value over time.
If you’re doubting how ubiquitous Copilot and other AI tools will become in the workplace, consider this: It took seven years for 100 million users to begin using the internet. To reach that same milestone, it took Facebook 4.5 years and ChatGPT only two months. The AI wave is coming and quickly. There’s simply no stopping it.
A Strategic Plan For Microsoft 365 Copilot Readiness
Acquiring a Copilot license is one small step on the road to the safe and strategic use of AI in the workplace. Before letting employees begin using Copilot, organizations need to become AI ready by completing the following four steps:
1. Educate leadership on AI and Copilot. The first step of a successful Microsoft 365 Copilot readiness journey is to get full leadership buy-in. Leaders need to understand the capabilities of both AI generally and Copilot specifically. Identify specific use cases across the organization and what roles would benefit the most from an AI assistant.
2. Complete a technical Copilot readiness assessment. This is a big hurdle for companies when opting for AI. Data needs to be in the right place for Copilot to access and be useful to people. At the same time, organizations need to ensure only the appropriate data is accessible. For example, you don’t want users to have access to sensitive information such as employee salaries or information controlled by regulatory bodies.
In short, it’s essential to have proper access controls and policies around data retention and data sharing. Microsoft does offer a tool, Microsoft Purview, to help organizations manage, protect and govern data, but many organizations will also want to turn to a trusted third party to help with this high-risk aspect of AI readiness.
3. Have a plan for Copilot adoption. Even the most fully productive organizations can benefit from Copilot, but you can’t simply turn the tool on and expect to see amazing results. Leaders and employees alike must reevaluate their processes to identify where the tool can best accelerate productivity. What tasks eat up a lot of time? Where can Copilot help lighten the workload and free up employees to focus on higher-value tasks?
Additionally, to ensure widespread Copilot adoption, leaders must provide training on Copilot and its capabilities. Training should include prompt engineering—the quality of the prompts you feed into Copilot directly impacts the quality of the tool’s output. A great tool is Microsoft’s Copilot Lab, a portal that offers education on prompt engineering, including many specific scenarios.
4. Align on short- and long-term goals for Copilot. Organizations should know what they’re hoping to achieve with Copilot. Increased productivity, fewer meetings, more rapid response to sales leads and smoother collaboration are just a few examples. Have goals in mind for the short- and long-term, then take advantage of the Copilot dashboard to track the tool’s productivity impact. It provides a number of useful metrics, such as active users, what Copilot features they’re using, hours saved and more.
The time is now to take action and get ready for Copilot. Two years from now, organizations that have used Copilot from the beginning will have realized impressive productivity gains. What’s more, throughout that entire time, the Copilot tool will just keep improving, becoming an increasingly more powerful productivity accelerator.

title: How Kate Middleton ‘KateGate’ Memes Mutated Into Conspiracy Frenzy
text:
The internet is reflecting on the Kate Middleton “KateGate” frenzy after the Princess of Wales released a video announcing her cancer diagnosis, putting an end to the memes and conspiracy theories — most of them, anyway.
In the wake of the announcement video, the jokes stopped being funny, and the endless speculation gave way to sympathy and guilt.
Some columnists took to scolding the public for the collective conspiracy frenzy. UK tabloids and royalists returned to their favorite pastime — criticizing Prince Harry and Meghan Markle.
Some commentators countered by highlighting the bizarre PR decisions made by the Palace, such as releasing a clumsily edited photo (supposedly taken by Prince William), then allowing Kate Middleton to take the blame for altering said photo.
Many viewed the excesses of “KateGate” as reflective of the current iteration of the internet, in which news, memes and conspiracy theories have melded together, mashed into content paste.
While Kate herself was rarely the butt of the joke, Prince William absolutely was, and the internet didn’t hold back.
While the UK government have blamed the phenomenon on Russian and Chinese troll farms, the trajectory and spread of “KateGate” seemed fueled by a subversive, mischievous compulsion to humiliate the powerful; English-speaking internet users didn’t need to be tricked into making fun of the Palace.
Mercilessly mocking an institution that typically enjoys a great deal of deference and respect — particularly from the British media — was key to the appeal.
How Did The ‘KateGate’ Memes And Conspiracies Begin?
Writing for the internet culture newsletter Garbage Day, Ryan Broderick took a deep dive into the origins of “KateGate” and found that the first #KateIsMissing hashtag could be traced back to a devoted group of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle fans known as the “Sussex Squad.”
Toward the end of January, the Squad kindled the first flames of concern, and kept the conspiracy theory warm until it was ready to be released into the mainstream, which was the end of February, right about the time that Prince William canceled a royal engagement citing a “personal matter.”
From there, the story entered popular discourse, as the jokes around Kate recovering from cosmetic surgery, a bad haircut, or hiding out at the Glasgow Willy Wonka fiasco took over the internet.
As amusing as they were, memes carried the conspiracy theories into the mainstream.
Just as the discourse was dying out, the Palace rekindled the flame, releasing the now-infamous Mother’s Day photo, which was promptly rejected by major news agencies, giving those conspiracy theories a major plausibility boost.
Suddenly, Kensington Palace was no longer viewed as a “trusted source,” giving way to endless speculation, as the public wondered why the Palace couldn’t provide a clear, unaltered photo of Kate Middleton.
The public already held a deep distrust of the palace, having seen the tragic fate of Princess Diana and the revelations of Prince Harry and Meghan Markle, who exposed the rot beneath the polished exterior.
Netflix’s The Crown dramatized the messy family history of the royals, inspiring throne-watchers to imagine the next phase of the soap opera.
The UK tabloids normalized rabid gossip and “mean girl” commentary around the royal family after Meghan Markle spoke out against palace officials, who allegedly denied her mental health treatment after she experienced suicidal thoughts.
After Markle spoke out, Piers Morgan accused her of lying on Good Morning Britain, and Jeremy Clarkson wrote an unhinged op-ed for The Sun, in which he fantasized about publicly humiliating Markle.
The direction the #KateIsMissing narrative took reflects how the public views the male heirs to the throne, and the fate of the women who enter the orbit of the Palace.
In the absence of information, internet users essentially created fan-fiction, speculating on what might be going wrong with Kate and Prince William’s marriage, boosting an infidelity rumor from 2019 and turning William’s alleged mistress, Rose Hanbury, into a meme; the rumor even made it to Steven Colbert, who amplified it to an even wider audience.
Hanbury's lawyers have since sent Colbert a notice demanding a retraction, but the rumor has already spread across the world, even sparking accusations that Hanbury’s luxurious home contains looted Chinese artifacts.
The ‘KateGate’ Memes Are Overtaken By Conspiracy Theories
The “KateGate” memes were fun, until they weren’t.
By the time a grainy video of Kate and William at a farm shop in Windsor was released, social media users were actively looking for clues and signs of deception, and the heavily pixelated footage only added to the suspicion.
Kate Middleton’s most recent video, in which she announces her cancer diagnosis, is clearly shot, and verified by the BBC.
However, conspiracy theorists are beginning to pick apart details in the video, such as Kate’s ring seemingly “disappearing” because of motion blur, and some are even dismissing the video as AI-generated.
Generative AI Made Everything Worse
Generative AI played a major role in amplifying the ‘KateGate’ conspiracies, and remains a major factor in their continuation.
Once the pixelated video of Kate and William’s farm shopping trip was released, commentators published screenshots “unblurred” by AI, which went viral on X (Twitter) and TikTok.
AI “unblurring” is highly inaccurate, as once image data has been lost, it cannot be restored. Generative AI “unblurs” grainy images by filling in the gaps with its own generative output — it does not restore lost data, it replaces it.
Hence, the AI “unblurred” two distinctly different faces, and neither resembled Kate. It didn’t seem to matter that two separate faces highlighted the AI’s inaccuracy, as conspiracy theorists and commentators were either willing to dismiss evidence that went against the #KateIsMissing narrative, or unaware of the limitations of the technology.
The rise of generative AI in image and video creation has proved a gift to conspiracy theorists, as crystal-clear video can now be dismissed as fakery, without resorting to weirder, more elaborate explanations, such as clones and body doubles.
The monumental PR blunders made by the Palace, combined with today’s conspiracy-heavy media landscape, resulted in “KateGate” mutating out of control.

title: Zoom Wants To Be Your One-Stop Work Platform, Plus, More DEI Closures
text:
Click here to get on the newsletter list!
How often have you found yourself using some sort of AI companion at work? Perhaps it’s the nature of the work I do, but I still take notes by hand during meetings (yes, I’m holding on to my physical reporter’s notebook like there’s no tomorrow) and spend most of my day talking to sources or writing stories (no AI there, that’s for sure).
That’s not to say there aren’t some great uses: AI-powered transcription services are helpful, and I’ve seen AI companions on calls to take meeting notes at work.
Like it or not, AI is becoming increasingly integrated in our jobs. On Monday, Zoom released “Zoom Workplace,” its answer to Microsoft’s Office 365 and Google’s Workspace programs. Its pitch is that its AI companion, launched in September, will help users work across offerings that include a meetings tab, document folders for team chats and more personalization options (think portrait lighting illuminating from the Zoom app).
The new tools have been in the works since October, when Forbes profiled founder and CEO Eric Yuan, who spoke about the company’s product expansion. But it’s entering a crowded field: Apart from Microsoft’s and Google’s offerings, more specialized project management platforms like Monday.com and Asana are scooping out their market share.
Still, there are some benefits in integrating work on one platform, saving time jumping between apps or tabs. A 2022 Harvard Business Review study found that workers toggled between tabs roughly 1200 times a day, adding up to nearly four hours of additional work. The combination of AI and more all-in-one platforms could help users save time.
Microsoft, for instance, says the most efficient users of its AI companion product Copilot save 30 minutes each day for a total of 10 hours a month. Average users, meanwhile, only saved 14 minutes each day, or five hours a month.
I don’t know how efficient I would be, but personally, I can get behind saving time when it comes to work. Hope you find ways to do the same this week.
WORK SMARTER
Practical insights and advice from Forbes staff and contributors to help you succeed in your job, accelerate your career and lead smarter
Pre-hire tests are on the rise. Know when to walk away from a job application.
How do you balance “loud-budgeting,” or talking about money and personal finance, while at work? Here’s how to say “no” to the extra spend while not missing out on networking opportunities.
Feeling lonely at work can be demoralizing and at times, even unproductive. Here’s how to beat it.
Having too many work friends can lead to unhealthy competition. But they can also help you advance in your own career.
Planning a much-needed vacation? Maybe a solo trip is in the cards. Here’s how to do it without feeling lonely.
CAREER ADVICE Q&A
Jon Stross, cofounder and president of Greenhouse, a provider of applicant tracking systems that employers use in recruiting, spoke with Forbes about who is using AI in the application process and how to avoid being overwhelmed by the increasing number of applicants per job at the beginning of your career. Excerpts from our interview have been condensed and edited for clarity.
How are candidates using AI?
It’s famously difficult to know. There's not a perfect algorithm that tells you that [someone] used ai. There's maybe two main use cases: One is writing a resume or cover letter using AI, so you can make your experience more personalized to the job much quicker. And then the other one is there's some services out there that will discover jobs and actually apply for you so you can apply to like 50 jobs at once.
Oh wow, how are you seeing that in the data?
There's like one candidate who applied to like 30 jobs in under a minute.
And are these effective? Are candidates getting hired?
It depends. The overall trend we do have some data on is that applications per job have really gone [up] by a lot over the last year. It's easy to point and say “oh, that's AI!” But it also [tells us something] about this part of the economy. The whole economy doesn’t use Greenhouse; it tends to be knowledge workers and tech companies. That part of the economy hit a peak in early 2022, and now it's been two straight years of slowing down, less venture capital and more layoffs. So when jobs do open, they get a lot of applicants. Technology has made it easier to discover and apply to jobs, but also it's just a fact of how many people are looking versus how many jobs are open.
What does that mean for the job-seeker’s experience?
From the candidate perspective, it means you're applying to lots of jobs and not hearing anything. There's the pure numbers: If a company gets 330 applications, they're not going to respond. They're not going to read every single one. That's very frustrating.
And for companies?
Employers will try to ask questions they can use either to auto-reject or auto-advance candidates—there are knockout questions, like if you don't have a visa. They'll also have questions that say, ‘Ooh, if anybody answers these questions in this way, ought to advance them and look at them first.’ Typically, they look at referrals first, and they'll certainly look at internal candidates first.
So how are people getting past the hundreds of applicants and getting hired? Are we back to the days of coffee chats and finding someone to be an internal referral?
That's certainly a good strategy! Greenhouse works with a lot of really high profile companies. Guess what? A lot of people want to work for those companies. We have companies getting like 10,000 applications for a single internship. There's a lot of great companies out there. Don't limit yourself just to the famous ones.
TOUCH BASE
News from the world of work
The U.S. House of Representatives is shutting down its diversity office as the newest spending bill passed on Saturday closed the House Office of Diversity and Inclusion. It will be replaced with a broader Office of Talent Management. Its closure was criticized by multiple Congressional groups. “Eradicating efforts that promote diversity and inclusion could reduce opportunities for staff of color, creating further barriers to representation in a body that already does not adequately reflect the diversity of the country it represents,” said a joint statement by the Congressional Black Associates, the Congressional Asian Pacific American Staff Association, the Congressional Hispanic Staff Association and the Senate Black Legislative Staff Caucus.
It may soon get easier—or at least a bit faster—for employers to hire workers based internationally, as AI tools ease the process of onboarding and writing employment contracts for “employers of record” in far-flung locales. Forbes’ Jena McGregor has the scoop about one such firm that just launched, Borderless AI, with $27 million in seed funding, co-founded by early Lyft investor Sean Aggarwal and entrepreneur Willson Cross.
Credit card company Deserve is reportedly looking into a sale as the fintech market slows. If you work for a company that may be considering a sale or has just been recently acquired, here are tips on how you can help protect your job.
Meet Forbes’ inaugural list of America’s top lawyers: Highlights include Yvette Ostolaza, the first Hispanic female leader of any Am Law 100 firm, and Roberta Kaplan, the founder of Time’s Up legal defense fund, which provides legal support to victims of workplace sexual harassment and discrimination.
VIDEO
This Iranian-born billionaire who helped take NASA back to the moon talks about building his companies’ cultures through the “ICE” principles.
NUMBER TO NOTE
Less than 12
That’s the total number of employees reportedly left at athletic wear company Outdoor Voices, whose founder and former CEO Tyler Haney is a part of the 2016 30 Under 30 Retail and E-Commerce class. Known for its viral workout dress (a 2021 must for hot-girl walks), the company told corporate employees it would be laying off 80% of its employees, abruptly closing down all of its 16 stores and leaving retail employees with no severance package. It is now facing bankruptcy, according to a Sourcing Journal report.
