title: Council Post: 4 Ways AI Can Empower Modern FP&A Teams
text:
Hunter Madeley, CEO Vena.
Traditionally risk-averse, finance teams continue to be slow in joining the AI train. When my organization Vena surveyed 175 finance professionals in 2021, only 7% were using artificial intelligence (AI) in their FP&A practices. In 2023, when we did another survey at our annual user conference, a full 74% still hadn’t implemented any AI tools into their immediate team.
Considering the growing popularity of AI across business functions, those numbers are very telling. And the truth is, finance teams are missing out.
Because finance teams are also uniquely positioned to benefit from AI—especially more recent advancements in generative AI. They’re not only the keepers of much of their organization’s most critical data, but they’re also making essential data-driven decisions every day to help guide their businesses forward.
AI can help translate those numbers into useful insights faster. It can also free up teams to spend less time recording and manipulating data—and more time expanding their strategic planning efforts instead.
But finance teams aren’t wrong to tread carefully when it comes to AI. With the right human oversight, though, there are plenty of ways AI promises to empower FP&A teams.
I’m seeing four main functions that are enabling leading-edge finance teams already as they explore AI’s game-changing potential. Each has game-changing potential—but there are potential risks to look out for as well.
1. Offer Self-Serve Insights
In their efforts to service the rest of the business, FP&A teams—as the keepers of the company’s data—are constantly answering questions, filling requests for financial data and tracking down critical details. This can be time-consuming and take away from their day-to-day tasks.
AI takes out the intermediary, offering the opportunity for self-serve insights. With the help of natural language processing, stakeholders can simply use everyday language to ask AI a question—and it will dig through the data to answer almost immediately. All of which frees up FP&A teams to concentrate on more strategic tasks.
Potential Risk: AI can sometimes be prone to “hallucinations” or mistaken outputs that are factually or contextually incorrect. You can ensure your stakeholders get the right answers to their questions, though, through responsible human oversight.
2. Generate Financial Models
In the past, generating financial models was a time-consuming task. With AI, it takes a lot less time. Finance teams that would previously create multiple scenarios manually through Excel no longer need to do that kind of repetitive work.
Not only does that save time for finance teams, but it also means they’re always working with the most current information to facilitate better and more agile decision-making and planning.
Potential Risk: Low-quality data can skew your results or create inaccurate or unreliable models—impacting the validity of your scenario planning and potentially leading to faulty insights. By ensuring your data is clean—and making sure you investigate what went into the model before you base important decisions on it—you’ll help build better results.
3. Forecast Future Results
It may not be a crystal ball, but AI has proven to be a powerful tool for helping FP&A teams forecast the future.
Rather than relying exclusively on historical data and manual calculations to forecast future sales, cash flow and the like, predictive analytics and machine learning tools make it possible to forecast using real-time data from across the organization. This means teams can keep on top of the most recent risks to their business and make up-to-the-moment predictions.
Potential Risk: Your historical data may have inherent biases baked in. And if you use that data to train your AI algorithm, your AI results could end up biased too. This can lead to flaws in your forecasts. Having a human check for bias can help ensure you have a clear view forward.
4. Spot Outliers in the Data
Finally, AI is particularly adept at flagging anomalies and changes in the data. And that can be a big help for busy finance teams—whether it’s noticing a mistake in the data or pointing to a trend that’s just beginning to emerge.
Humans make errors. It’s true of all of us, and it’s especially true for those strapped for time, trying to meet a deadline or working with large amounts of data. Those same circumstances can make it more difficult for teams to notice early anomalies in the numbers as well. These oversights can cause teams to miss signs of a future market trend or potential business threat.
Potential Risk: In this case, it’s AI that’s identifying the potential risks—but human oversight can come in handy for other reasons, too. Because once an outlier is identified, it takes human judgment to do something about it—whether that means double-checking a mistake or following up on an emerging trend.
Taking Finance To The Next Level
For teams that embrace it, AI is proving to be a catalyst—propelling finance leaders even further down a path they’ve been navigating for years. A path to becoming more fully realized strategic business partners—not just creating financial statements and reports, but pushing forward the analysis and insights that drive business growth.
The right AI tools can help make that journey easier and faster than ever. Finance teams just need to take the first step and embrace the opportunities AI brings—and learn to mitigate for the risks as well.

title: Why People Are The Core Of An AI Team
text:
AI systems are machines. There’s no debate around the central proposition that Artificial Intelligence (AI) and its Machine Learning (ML) engine power stems from software-driven computing devices which are essentially machine brains driven by algorithmic logic.
But really, it’s the people in an AI team that make the difference. If an intelligence team isn’t made up of the right mix of data scientists, business logic specialists, lower function systems administrators & higher tier systems architects… and even commercial function representatives such as salespeople and project managers, plus of course software application developers, then it’s not going to be a good team.
It’s a people thing
At present, we’re seeing a two-speed approach to the enterprise adoption of AI, with some organizations racing to implement solutions in an effort to generate rapid Return on Investment (ROI). At the same time, others are taking a longer-term view, hoping to reap future benefits based on investments made now. Regardless of where an organization maybe on its AI journey, it’s vital that the most important foundation of any AI strategy is not overlooked – that is people.
“Today we know that AI implementations face many of the same challenges as their technology predecessors and at present, most organizations aren’t thinking enough about the human element of their planned strategies,” proposed Alex McMullan, CTO International at data storage platform company Pure. “Technology's not always the problem, it can be come down to people - and when it comes to AI, this is very apparent. Part of the people problem is apparent in the AI skills shortage, where a lack of skilled data scientists, data engineers, platform engineers and other relevant professionals is hindering progress and adding to its cost. Salaries for AI professionals are at a premium right now and can account for up to 35% of project costs.”
Because another element of the people problem is managing AI data professionals in the right way so they are able to produce useful outcomes and drive efficiencies, McMullan thinks that the problem is compounded. We know that an AI model is only as good as the data that goes into it, which is in turn a people problem. If we also remember that biases can be introduced into algorithms resulting from the use of poor data bias, it’s easy to see why we need to think of professional people first… and then, professional AI second.
“As we move to the next wave of broader AI adoption, it’s an ideal time for organizations to conduct a detailed analysis of what is needed in terms of people, compute, storage infrastructure and data to deliver scalable projects that generate real ROI. It’s vital that any organisation considering an AI implementation invest in the right resources and technologies designed for the future to guarantee success,” said Pure’s McMullan.
Arguably well placed to comment on this issue is Human Resources (HR), financials and planning software specialist company Workday.
Tasks first, jobs second
“Building any AI function starts with developing an understanding of the workplace tasks and individual use cases that you are trying to achieve,” said Workday chief technology officer (CTO) Jim Stratton. “We use copilots internally written in our own proprietary software language [Workday XpressO is essentially an object-oriented wrapper for SQL database queries combined with a page builder] and external technologies in this space too. The challenge is, AI-centric copilots are good at coding, but they’re not so good at software engineering and being able to appreciate the human need behind any given implementation of AI.”
For Stratton and team, the development and implementation of AI is not just to accelerate job functions, it is about automation in a broader sense to enable software engineering to deliver applications that work across more world regions, to scale and grow better, to work with improved data safety (and eradicate AI bias), to present better integration capabilities and, of course, to offer more functions.
But why would AI help developers to integrate better? Stratton explains this point succinctly. Say one application needs to connect to another, a function often executed via the use of an Application Programming Interface (API), technology elements that act as a ‘glueing’ bond between apps and data services; here we see a developer able to use AI to shoulder the data mapping (to understand the format, shape, schema structure & syntax of the data) involved and make the whole process happen more accurately and more rapidly.
“Because our implementation of AI at Workday across HR, financials and planning solutions is often a question of working with other workplace systems, putting the human element into our approach to AI is fundamental to what we do,” said Stratton. “As we now work to elevate individuals to more strategic work tasks, we will always start AI projects with a people-centric mindset from the developers that create it to the users that use it. You can’t build highly distributed, highly available, high-performance systems (like ours) automatically, no software engineer in this space is going to be replaced by a copilot anytime soon.”
The point made here is clear, if we think about the implementation of a finance and HR system, it is connected to hundreds of other enterprise software systems covering revenue, employee benefits and onward to sales and marketing and so on. In many organizations, Stratton reminds us that that’s a very fragmented ecosystem with hundreds (or thousands) of applications to connect to. As we stand today, he is adamant that keeping the human factor at the fore in any AI implementation is tablestakes, first base and ground zero.
Chief AI officer (CAIO) at IFS is Bob De Caux. As a cloud enterprise software company with a key platform focus on ERP and related disciplines across Field Service Management & Enterprise Service Management, IFS has a vested interest and skill set aligned to AI team building and development. Agreeing with many of the sentiments and insights expressed here so far, De Caux says that from his viewpoint, a key part of building AI solutions is building the user experience to put around AI and people are crucial for getting that right.
“It's not such an issue when you're automating processes, but for a number of our industry use cases a human is still in the loop making decisions, with AI providing decision support,” said De Caux. “Therefore it's critical that we deliver AI outputs in a way that builds trust and confidence in what is often a non-technical user, which means finding a way to explain why AI models are making decisions, providing transparency into the data being used in the process and translating highly quantitative results into something with business meaning. Building that explainability and transparency framework to meet user needs is a very human venture.”
People first, data second, then AI
If we explain that people, processes, data and information provenance, work systems and task mining all come first, that doesn’t stop us still having the data use case argument front and center of this discussion. Because one of the biggest fears surrounding AI and automation is that machines are equipped to replace the workforce en masse, and we’re eventually all going to lose our jobs to robots and an array of AI systems manning assembly lines and customer inquiries, it’s important to remember that the reality is a lot more nuanced - and not nearly as intimidating.
This is the opinion of Richard Jones, VP for Northern Europe at data streaming platform company Confluent.
“In automating routine tasks, AI both creates new opportunities and enhances existing roles – I see it helping make people more rounded, skilled employees. Taking on the burden of tedious admin frees employees to focus on more complex, creative and strategic tasks that add value to the business,” said Jones, speaking to press &v analysts in London this spring. “I see job roles gradually evolving and placing more emphasis on informed decision-making and human interaction – allowing employees to upskill as they grow into these evolving responsibilities. But AI does more than just enhance existing roles; we’re seeing it create entirely new roles, such as prompt engineers, machine learning developers and data scientists.”
Talking about how smart use of data can elevate AI to higher levels, Jones reminds us that AI can sift through extensive datasets to deliver highly personalized experiences, meeting the rising expectations of consumers.
“Through leveraging data streaming technologies, this personalization can even occur in real-time, resulting in customer service applications that respond accurately, in a human way and in the moment,” said Jones. “AI, with the assistance of humans, holds the promise of significantly elevating customer experiences. AI-driven chatbots and virtual assistants offer immediate assistance around the clock, efficiently handling common queries and issues without human intervention. This instantaneity has the potential to greatly heighten the customer experience, while simultaneously freeing up people to address the more intricate and sensitive matters that do require human intervention.”
We want human AI
We know that businesses have reported improved customer satisfaction metrics following the integration of AI into their customer service workflows, underscoring technology's ability to augment rather than diminish the human touch – that’s if employees are willing to work alongside AI.
The people first (and indeed data first) AI message may continue to resonate for a significant period this decade as we work to engineer AI services into our enterprise operations layers, into our workflows and into our lives. Perhaps the question will soon be - when someone tells you there’s a new AI service bubbling up - great, how human is it?

title: Author Post: The Gaming Industry’s Edge in the Artificial Intelligence Revolution
text:
Since its foundation, the gaming industry has been a leader in technological innovation, pushing forward and embracing or creating new technologies.
Artificial intelligence (AI) has been part of gaming since the early days of arcade games. It has evolved from simple decision-making processes in games like Galaga to complex systems that power today’s large and immersive gaming worlds. The way we use AI today in game development gives us a peek into the future of this emerging technology.
How Today’s Games Use AI
Today, AI is not just an add-on but a key part of game development. It creates a more immersive and interactive experience for players. Developers use this technology to breathe life into non-playable characters (NPCs), making them seem real and encouraging interaction within the game.
Ubisoft, for example, uses AI to generate real-time text responses between players and NPCs. Yet, this only represents a small fraction of what AI can do with NPCs. With the way that AI is developing today, there may soon come a day when AI programs are playing the game just like their human companions.
But AI does more than improve dialogue. It can quickly create large digital environments, handle complex data, and simulate realistic environmental effects. This significantly changes the gaming experience.
These expansive digital realms rely on AI to manage vast amounts of data, coordinate interactions between players, and simulate ecosystems teeming with NPCs. This enables video games to provide a sense of realism and depth that would be very difficult without AI’s computational power and data management capabilities.
What AI Games Learn From Customers
AI’s potential goes beyond gaming. Similar to how Amazon and Netflix use customer data to make recommendations, gaming AI uses player behavior to inform game development and marketing strategies. This, in turn, opens new opportunities for growth. Additionally, AI can use this data to provide business leaders with a map of their organization’s issues and opportunities while guiding them to sustainable solutions that push their business forward.
A recent study from IDC reports returns of $3.50 on every $1 invested into new AI technology. These kinds of advances illustrate the gaming industry’s penchant for adopting the latest technology to see how it can improve their player’s experience. Indeed, by examining the new technology adopted by the gaming industry, business leaders from across different industries open a window into the future.
We can observe how people play with these new technologies in their games to see what’s on the horizon.
Toward an AI-Native Future
Businesses that proactively adopt industry-changing innovations gain a significant edge over their competitors. Twenty years ago, the digital transformation ushered in major changes across global industries. Today, however, the company that invests in AI will reap the benefits of this industry disruption.
The rise of AI-native gaming companies is anticipated to be a major shift. It’s leading to a new era of virtual collaboration worldwide. These companies are recognized for their advanced technology and ability to analyze data. This allows game developers and publishers to optimize the creation and operation of games in ways we couldn’t imagine before.
While many might look to Silicon Valley’s largest tech giants for answers about AI, those tech giants do not hold a monopoly on this emerging machine learning technology. As the gaming industry uses AI more and more, it’s paving the way with innovative structures and creative processes that can be applied to other sectors. The lessons we learn from creating, developing, and operating AI-driven platforms will be useful across industries.
In a world that’s increasingly defined by AI, the gaming industry’s journey with this technology is a great example. It not only improves the gaming experience but also shows how other industries might use AI to improve human capabilities and experiences.
As we move towards a future dominated by AI, the gaming industry’s path acts as a guide and a driving force, pushing forward the joint evolution of society and technology.

title: Council Post: The Generative AI Opportunity For High Tech
text:
Syed is Accenture’s High Tech global lead, helping clients with growth strategy, reinvent their business and optimize supply chain.
According to recent research by my company, Accenture, in which I'm the semiconductor industry global lead, 77% of high-tech executives see generative AI (GenAI) as a key lever in their reinvention strategy. Yet, only 58% of them see it as a top contributor to revenue growth. This gap can be attributed to a lack of understanding of GenAI and how to integrate the technology for revenue growth.
In a previous article, I discussed GenAI use cases and best practices for high-tech companies to start adopting the technology. In this piece, I’ll dive deeper into the potential for GenAI to transform the entire high-tech value chain and the imperatives to follow to successfully implement the revolutionary technology.
From Transforming The Value Chain To Driving Revenue Growth
There are plenty of opportunities for high-tech companies to apply generative AI to transform every step of their value chain. High-tech supply chains are very complex, and the slightest disruptions can have impacts measured in months. Supply chain resilience can be improved by using LLMs (large language models) for due diligence and end-to-end contract management as well as by giving stakeholders the visibility they need to react much faster.
It is also possible to enhance the productivity of a manufacturing operation by leveraging generative AI for rapid prototyping and product design during initial production, as well as using synthetic data to improve quality, reduce waste or improve efficiency by identifying breakdowns and bottlenecks early on. Lower down the value chain; field technicians stand to benefit from context-based information that can assist them in completing their work faster and more accurately.
But the benefits are not limited to optimizing operations; they can help drive revenue growth as well. Sales teams, for example, can use gen AI assistants to bring up the most current and relevant information about customers, ranging from recent communications across channels to past transactions and stated intents, effectively improving opportunity conversions. Similarly, customer support interactions can be turned into opportunities by having assistants bring up relevant new services for cross-selling and upselling. These benefits can extend to downstream organizations by delivering deep insights that can help guide customer success managers and SMB partners.
Creating A Strong Ecosystem Around AI
An ecosystem approach can deliver great results—just look at the semiconductor industry and its fabless model or how software and platforms companies have leveraged the investments of the telco industry to thrive. Because building out AI offerings is a huge undertaking—it's costly and requires extensive infrastructure—I'd strongly recommend high-tech businesses create an intentional ecosystem that leverages each stakeholder's strengths and hedges against risks. The good news is that it is already happening.
For example, we helped Intel build downloadable AI reference kits to share with the open-source community, enabling developers to quickly optimize code to meet the increasing demands of AI workloads. Within 15 months, the joint team trained about 220 developers on the enterprise potential of AI analytics technology. Similarly, HPE broadened its GreenLake portfolio, partnering with German AI company Aleph Alpha to offer GreenLake for LLMs. This allows customers to build their own AI models using their own data without paying for supercomputers because the offering runs on HPE’s own Cray XD supercomputers, which have an AI-native architecture.
5 Imperatives For Implementation
• Focus on talent and reinvent the way your people work by adapting operating models fit for the gen AI era, with a strong focus on talent development and continuous learning and skilling. Building competencies across functions to fully understand the impact of generative AI on people as well as developing the capabilities to provide them with the continuous learning needed to embrace generative AI will play a key role in how the technology is received.
• Lead responsibly by approaching AI intentionally and strategically. Ensure all AI actions—from design to deployment and use within the organization—drive value while being aware of and protecting against the risks of AI, such as bias or infringement of intellectual property and data privacy. This means taking a close look at the data being used by your models and doing extensive testing before deploying solutions.
• Establish an AI-enabled digital core by enabling a modern data platform, rearchitecting applications to be AI-ready and adopting a flexible architecture that allows the use of multiple models across your ecosystem. According to our research, most high-tech executives believe GenAI will lead to organizations modernizing their tech infrastructure.
• Plan for continuous reinvention. Generative AI is a technology complex in nature that requires the right capital, talent and multiple years to implement successfully, so a long-term plan (spanning years, not quarters) broken down into steps is needed to make progress while setting realistic expectations.
• Focus on value by staying away from siloed use cases and prioritizing business capabilities across the entire value chain based on return on investment. Client value should be at the core of every business capability you choose to reinvent with Gen AI. Investments should be pursued in two categories: table stakes investments that offer radical efficiency on one end and strategic bets that offer truly novel advantages on the other.
Leading As Adopters And Enablers
Overall, GenAI has the potential to transform the entire high-tech industry value chain by optimizing processes, reducing costs, improving customer satisfaction and driving revenue growth. As the technology continues to advance, high-tech companies that embrace and integrate generative AI into their operations will have a competitive advantage in the market as both adopters and enablers of the technology.

title: Council Post: AI For Accessibility Means AI For All—No Magic Needed
text:
FindGood.tech - Fmr Executive Sony, Qualcomm, MP3.com, Journalist | Vice Chair, StartUp San Diego | SD Police Foundation "Women in Blue."
Imagine a world where you suddenly lose your ability to hear. Your surroundings fall into eerie silence, conversations become mere gestures and your connection to the world begins to crumble. This was my reality when I experienced total hearing loss while at work, unable to hear my colleagues speak, mere inches away. Little did I know that this deafening silence had slowly crept up on me over the years due to a condition called otosclerosis, which calcified bones in my ears. A $7,000 investment later in the latest hearing-assisted devices, harnessing the power of artificial intelligence (AI), transformed my working life.
This opened my eyes (and ears) to the immense potential of AI, not only in addressing hearing loss but in revolutionizing countless aspects of our lives. Hearing aids of today are not simple microphones—they are bespoke to each sound, capable of anticipating, modulating and seemingly understanding the listener's environment.
They are paired with smartphones and in many use cases exceed the hearing potential most were born with, especially paired with technology from companies such as SonicCloud.
My journey, while deeply personal, reflects a broader societal shift. The rise of AI technology promises to liberate millions of people facing various limitations, with hearing loss affecting a staggering 48 million Americans.
However, what concerns me is the prevailing fear surrounding AI. According to Pew Research, 52% of Americans express heightened concerns about the increased use of artificial intelligence, a 14% increase from the previous year. Only 10% are excited about its prospects, while 36% feel ambivalent, mixed at best.
Given this mostly fear-fueled perception of AI, how can we move forward to realize the power of AI for accessibility and other healthcare innovations, especially in life sciences where so many cures stand to be discovered?
In my perspective, the real fear isn't AI itself but the fear of being sorted into a class of the haves and have-nots. Making things worse, tech culture tends to portray AI as mystical "magic," obscuring its accessible underlying theories. While applied AI is profoundly complex, the theories underlying it are not.
There are however excellent insights on AI from leaders at Spotify and IBM, who leverage external and employee communications to bridge gap.
Spotify CTO Gustav Soderstrom, an expert communicator, recently unraveled the basics of how an LLM works at an “all hands” employee meeting. The company also chose to post the internal talk on YouTube. His talk spoke about how AI is truly made to seem harder than it actually is.
Marina Danilevsky, a senior research scientist at IBM, explains simply why ChatGPT-4 is now so much better than ChatGPT-3 in a simple video.
While these may seem like simple videos on technology, they're actually something more powerful as they are strengthening social capability while creating brand affinity. Company communicators need accessible, relatable content to bring all along in the AI journey.
What Are Some Advanced Strategies For Communicating AI Implementation?
• Leadership involvement and storytelling: Have leaders share stories of AI augmenting their decision-making or productivity, thereby humanizing AI's potential impact. Google CEO Sundar Pichai often shares how AI is used to enhance Google products in ways that improve people’s daily lives, reinforcing the positive aspects of AI development. Google has been fairly active given its recent and promising developments on Gemini (formerly known as Bard).
• Peer advocates: Identify early adopters within the organization who can share their positive experiences with AI. Salesforce uses “Trailblazers” or in-house AI advocates (chief AI evangelist!) to share how AI tools like Einstein AI have empowered them to make smarter decisions and connect with customers more effectively.
• Ethical and transparent AI use: Provide transparency about how AI decisions are made, including any biases and how they are addressed. Accenture created an AI ethics committee that works on establishing AI guidelines and governance, ensuring all employees understand the ethical considerations in AI applications.
• Future skills and role evolution: Instead of simply reassuring job security, communicate specific plans for skills development and how roles will evolve with AI. Amazon’s "AI Ready" initiative is an example where the company invests in training programs to prepare its workforce for the future, including in areas impacted by AI.
Public Education Tools
For startups looking to educate their employees about AI without developing extensive in-house training programs, pointing to public education tools and resources can be an efficient and cost-effective strategy.
• Online courses and MOOCs: Platforms like Coursera and edX offer low-cost courses from universities and institutions around the world on AI and machine learning. Courses range from introductory to advanced levels. For example, "AI For Everyone" by Andrew Ng on Coursera is a nontechnical course that provides a broad introduction to AI. And Khan Academy's LLM Khanmigo and EdX are good examples of altruistic learning options for those feeling left behind.
• Udacity: Known for its tech-centric curriculum, Udacity offers Nanodegree programs in AI and machine learning, which are designed in collaboration with industry leaders. These programs are project-based, helping learners to gain practical experience.
• AI4ALL open learning: AI4ALL offers open-access lessons aimed at high school students but suitable for anyone interested in learning about AI's social implications and ethical considerations.
Additionally, organizing discussion groups where employees can share insights from these resources can further enhance understanding and mitigate concerns about AI implementation. Hera Hub, a national coworking space focused on women, is excellent at doing this and regularly holds programming for members where I teach a prompting workshop.
By pointing employees to these resources, small companies can facilitate self-directed learning and help make AI not only accessible but fun.
In closing, while I cherished my $7,000 hearing aids, I no longer use them thanks to AI-assisted robotic surgery. My hearing is near bionic, so I feel a bit like a hybrid-AI bot. We are at the beginning of accessibility revolution—no magic needed.

title: Council Post: The Non-Technologists Are The Compass For AI Creators
text:
Bob Pearson, Chair, The Next Practices Group and The Bliss Group.
Our brains are built to seek predictability. We like getting into a groove, so when something like generative artificial intelligence (AI) hits our shores, it feels like a tsunami has arrived and we were just fine, thank you, with 3- to 5-foot waves.
We don’t need to make it so complicated. All we need to do is break down how innovation normally occurs and why we have a role in how our world is shaped.
The World Intellectual Property Association is a good place to start. They define an inventor as someone who identifies an unmet need or a problem and then figures out the solution. That’s it. Funny how nothing in that statement says that you have to know how to code or have deep knowledge of AI or live in Palo Alto.
With that in mind, let’s take a minute and think of today’s world of AI news differently.
Non-Technologists’ Role In AI Development
The compass, which reacts to magnetic fields and tells us where we are going, is one of the most important devices to navigate where we are heading in life. Generative AI is symbolic of a magnetic field. Like a magnetic force, it pushes us to change how we think about tomorrow. It is unrelenting, and we should expect it to stay this way. You can’t stop a magnetic force, but you can harness it and become the arrow.
The great majority of us, the non-technologists, have the opportunity to partner with software programmers and point them in the right direction to disrupt a market or solve a new problem. We decide what problems we want to solve, whether it is building a new healthcare application to serve the needs of those battling a rare disease or a new way to pull data to create a corporate language model that tracks our firm’s reputation. Or just a better way to build a parking lot.
The non-technologists know what is needed in the world since we work directly with customers and employees worldwide every day. We must trust our instincts and join AI creators to imagine a better solution.
Sounds simple, so why doesn’t it happen regularly? It starts with how we make innovation more complex than it is in practice.
How To Navigate The World Of AI
The concept of innovation is pretty simple. It occurs when we think of something that is not available today. We may iterate on a past solution to improve it. We may mash up two products to create a new and better one. We may obsess over a customer pain point until we figure out the problem.
Our solutions will, unfortunately, sit there and age until they are irrelevant unless we can find partners who can make them come to life. Software and data science fulfill this role as our future partners.
This is step one: Find people who are creating the magnetic force while you serve as the arrow to build your own compass pointed toward a problem that will improve something in our world.
Step two relates to the noise inside our heads. Most of us love the status quo and change makes us uneasy. We don’t like disruption, even if we know the result may be an improvement. We’re thinking, “Can’t you just keep doing what we did last year?”
We are fearful of big bosses learning that we failed at a project. It is a fear that stops us well before we contemplate how we would structure a new idea, so it feels easier not to try. We are not as confident as we should be in our abilities to innovate, and we tell ourselves that our ideas are probably not that great. That’s our inside voice.
Here is reality: During a career of being willing to try new models anytime anywhere, I have learned quite the opposite is true. Some of the best partnerships occur between idea people and technologists who can push each other intellectually to create a new solution. Neither of us usually has “the answer,” but together, it is like chocolate and peanut butter.
Becoming A Compass
Every pilot is a learning that helps us iterate to the right place or realize we won’t get there in the near term. Not everything works, but every result offers insights.
Leaders of companies have more respect than you realize for those who disrupt the status quo. Your peers may not since they are often the antibodies to change, but the boss does. They are always thinking of how to gain an edge in the market. Stay strong.
The epiphany is to realize that it’s okay if you don’t code or know exactly how to use every new AI app. You are excellent at identifying unmet needs and establishing what the problem is. You are capable of finding a partner who can make this idea come to life.
In fact, as a non-technologist, you are the compass for the AI creator who needs your partnership to build a solution that will matter to the market. No inventors want to raise money, build a cool slide deck and then fail. We all want to succeed.
Partner and skip a generation or two of learning by mashing up your knowledge. Remember that the other half of AI innovation is all of us who don’t live in Silicon Valley. Let’s build the solutions we need together.

title: Council Post: From Risk To Reward: Ensure Your AI Is An Asset, Not A Liability
text:
Alok Kulkarni is Co-Founder and CEO of Cyara, a customer experience (CX) leader trusted by leading brands around the world.
In the past, customer service interactions took place between two individuals—the agent and the customer. Delivering a top-notch customer experience mainly involved training agents to interact empathetically with customers and resolve their issues. But in today’s era of self-service, everything has shifted. Thanks to advancements in artificial intelligence (AI), many customer issues can now be resolved without the help of human agents. From simple banking transactions to tracking order status, modern AI-powered chatbots and interactive voice response (IVR) systems can handle a variety of customer requests.
Unlike human representatives, AI bots are capable of offering round-the-clock support and managing numerous inquiries simultaneously. Gartner predicts that by 2026, conversational AI deployments in contact centers could reduce agent labor costs by up to $80 billion.
However, the benefits that these bots offer are not exclusive to organizations. Nearly 70% of customers today want—and expect—self-service options so they can resolve as many issues as possible on their own. But there is a caveat: When bots underperform or hinder customer service, they can easily become an organization’s worst nightmare.
When AI Goes Awry
Most people today know what it’s like when AI interactions go wrong. For instance, when you get stuck in the frustrating loop of confusing or incorrect responses from a chatbot or you’re not able to seamlessly switch from a bot to a human agent. Unfortunately, it can get much, much worse—just ask Air Canada.
One of the most prevalent and dire areas where conversational AI bots struggle is in understanding customer intent, which refers to what a customer aims to accomplish or the result they seek when interacting with an organization.
There are over 7,100 languages worldwide, along with numerous dialects, evolving slang and diverse writing and speech styles. Due to the complexity and diversity of ways in which people can express themselves, understanding customer intent can be a challenging task, even for humans. Now, imagine how difficult it is to ingrain such skills in bots. For instance, a customer wishing to return a T-shirt can phrase the request in multiple ways, such as:
• How can I get a refund on my shirt?
• Need refund on this shirt
• T-shirt is small and I want my $ back
Despite not explicitly using the word "return" in these requests, the chatbot must accurately grasp the customer's intent. This is a common stumbling block for chatbots—especially when the requests become more intricate or emotionally charged—as 74% of customers still think chatbots can’t handle complex questions. As a result, consumers sometimes find themselves disappointed with their chatbot experiences. When utilizing an AI-powered IVR system or a voice-enabled chatbot, additional variables come into play that introduce another layer of complexity, such as different accents, voices, languages, poor bandwidth or phone quality and background noises.
Beyond simply failing to establish customer intent, AI chatbots—especially when leveraging large language models (LLMs)—can also exhibit other flaws that raise concerns about their reliability.
Non-deterministic: Users may not receive consistent answers to the same question each time it is posed. This lack of predictability introduces an element of uncertainty, diminishing the trust users place in the chatbot's responses.
AI hallucinations: Generating factually incorrect or nonsensical responses. This poses a risk to the accuracy and credibility of the interactions.
Biases: Inadvertently generating racist, sexist or homophobic perspectives. These biases not only reflect poorly on the technology but also raise ethical concerns about the impact of AI on perpetuating harmful stereotypes and discrimination.
AI model drift: Responses gradually become less pertinent and comprehensible over time.
Recognizing and addressing these flaws is essential to responsibly develop and deploy AI-powered chatbots across any application.
Mastering The Machine: Ensuring Your AI Is An Asset
Chatbots typically use natural language understanding (NLU), a subset of AI, to interpret customer inputs. However, the effectiveness of chatbots relies heavily on the knowledge that fuels them. Given the intricate and diverse ways humans express their intent, substantial amounts of data are essential to properly train a chatbot to recognize the broad spectrum of inputs it encounters. This training data must consist of examples representing each intent, serving as the foundation for a model that enables the chatbot to identify and respond to each.
In addition to training chatbots on how to comprehend customer intent, organizations should also implement ongoing testing and optimization procedures to identify and address potential issues before customers encounter them or are negatively impacted by them. Effective chatbot testing assesses the bot's understanding of customer intent continuously as the chatbot matures and consumer input changes. This testing can be conducted at scale to ensure the chatbot's performance even in high-volume scenarios. It is also crucial for chatbot testing to assess the bot's functionality in the different channels it resides in, whether that is in a mobile app, within an IVR on a website, or on social platforms like Facebook Messenger. Adopting an automated and continuous chatbot testing approach not only enhances the chatbot's quality, ensuring it performs as anticipated, but also minimizes the workload on enterprise information technology (IT) teams.
The Key Ingredient For Successful AI Customer Service Experiences
In a future dominated by AI, organizations will undergo a major shift as considerable workloads transition from human interactions to AI-powered chatbots. But despite AI’s advancements, it still frequently falls short in handling complex customer tasks and interactions with the same effectiveness as real humans. Over 80% of consumers state that if they are having trouble with AI customer service tools, the availability of a human agent is critical to maintaining trust with that organization. That’s why human agents will continue to play a vital role, particularly in situations that require empathy and nuanced judgments.
While AI is undoubtedly reshaping the landscape of customer service, striking the right balance between AI and human touch is key to delivering a seamless and customer-centric experience. Organizations that recognize and embrace this need for augmentation will provide exceptional service and better foster lasting customer relationships—excelling above the rest.

title: Databricks Unveils An AI Model That Helps Businesses Build Their Own Models
text:
Databricks, an AI data and analytics company valued at $43 billion, unveiled a new language model on Wednesday—this one aimed at helping other companies build and train their own AI agents.
Called DBRX, the model will allow businesses to create custom artificial intelligence based on their own proprietary data. The company said it performs better than OpenAI’s GPT 3.5, but not the current GPT model that powers the popular ChatGPT. The software is open-sourced, like Meta’s LLaMA 2 model, so companies will be able to use it for free, but must pay if they want to use it with the Databricks cloud platform. The company charges pay-as-you-go fees for its tools, with discounts for committed usage.
“We think that open source just moves the industry forward. Companies don't want to get locked into different proprietary standards,” CEO Ali Ghodsi said during a briefing with reporters on Monday. “So it's actually also a competitive advantage for us business-wise.”
Databricks makes money by renting out tools to other companies for storing, collecting and governing data. The company—backed by Nvidia, Capital One and Andreessen Horowitz—was founded in 2013, but has flown high during the current AI boom. Earlier this month, the company said it generated more than $1.6 billion in revenue in the last fiscal year, representing 50% growth from the previous year. The company is widely expected to be soon headed to an initial public offering, though hasn’t provided a timeframe.
While much of the public imagination has been captured by consumer products like ChatGPT and Google’s Gemini, analysts say that many of the major benefits of artificial intelligence will be for businesses. McKinsey estimates generative AI’s boost on productivity could add between $2.6 trillion and $4.4 trillion in value annually to the global economy, enabling automation of up to 70% of business activities across almost all occupations by 2030. Meanwhile, OpenAI estimates 80 percent of jobs can incorporate generative AI capabilities into their workflows.
Databricks isn’t the only company offering tools for other companies to build custom large language models. Competitors include LangChain, backed by Sequoia and Benchmark, and Lightning AI, backed by Index Ventures and Bain Capital. Both OpenAI and Google also offer tools for creating specific-purpose LLMs.
The model is trained using a “mixture-of-experts” architecture, which assigns the work of generating answers to four different “experts” within the model—which each specialize in a different area, like literature or math—instead of relying on computation from the entire model. The idea is to speed up performance by requiring less processing.
The launch of this new product comes just eight months after Databricks acquired MosaicML, a generative AI platform, last July for $1.3 billion. That team was largely responsible for building the model, which is the first that Databricks has ever built from the ground up. However, the company did last year release a model called Dolly built on an existing model, EleutherAI’s Pythia—an experiment to show that a relatively old model could be easily customized and fine-tuned.
DBRX took about $10 million and two months to train on 3,000 Nvidia GPUs, Ghodsi said. The goal is for the model to help enterprise companies develop “world class” language models at lower costs. “I think 18 months ago you would have to spend $100 million to get a similar quality model,” Ghodsi told Forbes.

title: New Adobe Research: Generative AI Is Changing What Consumers Expect From Brands
text:
About a year ago, I spoke to Luc Dammann, President EMEA at Adobe, about some new research that Adobe had just published. The research found that consumers expect even better experiences from brands when economic conditions become more challenging.
Now, if you think about it, that makes complete sense. When their budgets are under pressure, consumers become even more discerning about where and with whom they spend their money.
However, according to the research, consumers didn’t just want lower prices and better experiences. The research also found that while consumers want brands to deliver those things they also wanted them to do so both responsibly and sustainably.
That piece came out out almost a year ago.
So, last week, in the run-up to Adobe Summit, which is currently taking place in Las Vegas, I caught up with Dammann again to see what had changed over the last year and to ask him how brands were getting on with their experience-led growth initiatives and delivering personalisation at scale.
He told me, “We remain in a context where brands are struggling with the fact that they have consumers who, no matter what, are digital-first, but also that the macro environment remains extremely uncertain.” He went on to say, “With the rise of technology and generative AI, in particular, consumers remain extremely sensitive to how brands are going to use the tech responsibly. These are the issues that are top of mind for all of the customers we are talking to at the moment.”
Reflecting on Dammann’s insights, you could argue that not much has changed in the last year.
But you’d be wrong.
Newly released research from Adobe suggests that, whilst consumers still have concerns about the responsible use of technology, the big thing that has changed over the last year is that the general public has embraced generative AI and is increasingly using it as a tool in their everyday lives.
According to Adobe’s recently released Age of Generative AI research, which surveyed 2,000 UK consumers over the course of February and March of this year, nearly three-quarters (73%) of UK consumers report that they have used generative AI in their personal lives.
These figures suggest that, beyond the headlines and the hype, generative AI has captured the interest of the general public.
But, digging into the research, what’s really interesting is how those surveyed consumers think that generative AI will also impact customer experience.
Here’s a summary of the relevant findings:
- 55% of retail shoppers say generative AI has already improved their online shopping experience,
- 49% of consumers said they would be more inclined to purchase from brands that use generative AI on their websites,

title: Council Post: How Contact Centers Can Transition From Deflection To Resolution
text:
Gadi Shamia is the CEO and cofounder of Replicant.
How can automation be leveraged to make contact centers more efficient? If you asked this five years ago, you’d find recommendations like "point callers to the right channel," "highlight your self-support options" or "assist agents to make them more productive." In other words, deflect.
To customer service leaders, these tactics are common knowledge, but so is the reality that these tactics often do not truly move the efficiency needle.
By no fault of their own, contact centers have been limited in how much they can accomplish with automation. The constraints of interactive voice response (IVR) and chatbots meant that service leaders had no choice but to use tactics like deflection to combat agent shortages, rising costs and increased customer demand.
Fortunately, the GenAI boom has made human-to-machine interactions mainstream while increasing the types of calls that can be automated. Now, automation is finally having the kind of impact on contact centers that ATMs once had on banking: end-to-end assistance for common customer requests.
As a result, service leaders no longer have to focus their efforts on squeezing more productivity out of agents, designing complicated routing trees or redirecting callers to channels other than the one they’ve already chosen. Instead, enterprises can use AI to fully resolve common customer issues without agent involvement, all while improving customer experience and delivering cost savings.
Resolving Customer Issues Gets To The Root Of CX Challenges
When automation is measured by deflection or containment success, it's not uncommon for contact centers to see only marginal improvements toward these pain points. But when automation resolves customer requests at scale, substantial improvements can be made in cost savings, customer satisfaction and their overall preparedness for unpredictable call spikes.
A high-resolution rate means that customer requests are being fully completed by automation and agents are receiving a significantly lower call volume for requests they previously spent time on. With AI, the flows that can be automated go far beyond simple routing and authentication tasks to include complex requests like payments, appointment scheduling and even roadside assistance.
A high-resolution rate implies that callers are getting an experience where they don’t feel the need to escalate to an agent. This gives callers natural conversations, the ability to correct themselves, low latency and more—all with no wait times, annoying phone trees or small talk.
When automation resolves requests end to end, the cost to complete each call is around 50% lower than agents or business process outsourcing with untold additional value coming from a better agent experience that features fewer mundane calls and more engaging interactions.
A resolution-based strategy means service leaders can focus less on finding day-to-day fixes for unpredictability and more on making every customer interaction better.
Pitfalls To Avoid When Pursuing A High-Resolution Rate
While a fail-fast strategy may work in other AI applications, it can negatively impact resolution rate and brand trustworthiness in customer service.
In February 2024, for example, Canada's Civil Resolution Tribunal ruled that Air Canada must fulfill a reimbursement to a customer erroneously promised a refund by the airline’s AI chatbot. The airline argued that it can’t be held responsible for any incorrect information that AI provides on its own. However, the Tribunal determined that it's incumbent upon companies "to take reasonable care to ensure their representations are accurate and not misleading."
Organizations that rush to resolve without first implementing the proper guardrails put their business at risk. Conversely, a 'wait-and-see' approach pushes your brand’s innovation horizon out while allowing competitors to gain an edge.
A balanced AI strategy takes into account the difficulty of designing an automation solution that can safely resolve calls at a high clip. This includes requisite features like a multi-model architecture to leverage the best available LLMs, a high capacity for flexibility to incorporate your business logic, and an enterprise level of scalability and security.
While solutions like contact center as a service (CCaaS) add-ons may allow you to configure AI on your own, it's important to note that they are limited in their conversation accuracy and flexibility. It's not unlikely that organizations may face limitations when attempting to resolve complex use cases and may receive a lower level of ongoing support and expertise.
Meanwhile, organizations that attempt to build a solution on their own may underestimate the complexity of the project. If this is a consideration, it's important to carefully analyze the resources of your organization to ensure this is a realistic pursuit. This way, you can better avoid cost overruns and resource-heavy maintenance responsibilities.
As more organizations partner with solution providers, ask prospective partners how they plan to mitigate risk in your strategy without delaying your timeline. Furthermore, be sure to discuss the customization potential of pre-built solutions for your business.
The Contact Center Of The Future
Gartner projects that 80% of organizations will apply generative AI to improve CX by 2025, resulting in a 20%-30% reduction in agents and the creation of new jobs to enable generative AI. I also expect that a reduction in tier-one agents will lead to the creation of an "expert class" of tier-two agents who will specialize in an industry or company and consider their job as a career, not a gig.
For service leaders, implementing a resolution-based automation solution in 2024 begins with connecting your contact center’s strategy with your enterprise’s strategy. Performing a call assessment is a great place to start.
A call assessment is an impactful exercise that analyzes the contact center’s data to show where your agents currently spend the most time. It uses AI to identify high-volume call flows that can be automated with a high-resolution rate as well as the savings to expect by doing so based on your current costs. More importantly, a call assessment makes it easy to tie the impact of resolution rate directly to business goals like net hiring savings, average hold times, CSAT and your ability to meet SLAs during call spikes.
Regardless of the approach, refocusing your automation strategy from one based on deflection to one focused on resolution can help lead to efficiency that benefits everyone involved.

title: Council Post: The Expectations Era: How AI Can Uplevel Customer Experience
text:
Stephen Hsu is Chief Product Officer of Calendly and a seasoned SaaS executive.
It’s an exciting time for B2B tech leaders, as AI holds tremendous potential to create more intuitive and seamless customer experiences. AI has entered the scene as customer expectations have increased for more and better functionalities delivered faster, as well as their zero tolerance for clunky user experiences.
While it’s tempting to build with AI as a sort of “race to the top,” it’s important to focus on applications that drive maximum user value. A recent Menlo VC report found that generative AI hasn’t fully delivered on the promise of meaningful transformation. Their research cites that because enterprises “have failed to create new workflows and behaviors, productivity feels limited.”
It’s crucial to strike a balance between the novelty of innovating with AI and its daily usefulness to make your product stickier and more differentiated. You’re not only improving productivity, but your partner ecosystem can also exchange data to make customers more effective against team goals.
Let’s explore four meaningful ways that AI can drive successful customer outcomes.
Make Complementary Products Work Better Together
When B2B SaaS products integrate, the goal is to create a better overall customer experience for their shared user base. A successful integration isn’t only convenient for customers; it can also make each product more valuable. A big opportunity for AI is to create an engagement layer that sits on top of multiple SaaS applications or systems of record.
Many SaaS companies aspire to be a system of record, but in reality, they’re sitting on their own data island. A more compelling use case for AI is to unify user data across multiple products, pulling it in and out of systems to create a more effective platform ecosystem. Data should flow bi-directionally between integrated partners in the ecosystem so customers can make more informed decisions faster. AI leveraging data from systems of record on the fly could reveal relevant information in a way that produces both qualitative and quantitative insights.
At a rudimentary level, AI could mitigate some of the workflow and challenges associated with partner integrations. Many products change their APIs or data models frequently, which breaks existing integrations and requires developers to fix them. AI could identify potential failures or issues and do the work to short-circuit faulty API integrations.
Reduce Mundane Tasks And Close The Loop
Most customers would be happier if their tech stack solved their most acute pain points. Take meetings, the ultimate unit of productivity and business growth, and yet also often the blame for lower worker satisfaction and engagement. But really, it’s the inefficiencies that are paining workers: 1 in 4 workers spend 3 to 4 hours a week scheduling meetings. Multiplying that with the hundreds of monthly meetings recruiters or salespeople schedule and removing that monotony would be one effective way to apply AI to a common business problem.
Beyond reducing mundane tasks, AI can be used to close the loop between integrated products. Embedded AI should understand the user’s typical workflow and configure the next step automatically based on the ultimate goal. Using the sales example above, AI could reference your history of customer interactions to generate a logical meeting agenda that would steer sellers to address pain points in real time, book the next meeting, take notes and create action items, all to expedite and help close more deals.
The opportunity for AI is that it isn’t confined by rigid automation logic that a human created. It knows to focus on the customer experience across any touchpoint, so it in theory can pull the relevant data at the right time and provide a consistent and proactive experience.
Improve How Leaders Prioritize
When it comes to influencing key decision-makers in 2024, you’re not just speaking to end-users but also business leaders. The B2B purchasing journey and customer expectations for software have evolved, impacting your product strategy. Leaders need to buy into your offering and extract full value from your software, making AI a smart facilitator.
A valuable application for AI is to surface key user insights for leaders and admins from the products their teams use most. Getting a leader’s view into the application’s data removes the reporting requirement from team members’ day-to-day workflows and ultimately improves productivity.
In-product AI could help your customers prioritize more effectively at a leadership level. Imagine a scenario where AI could help a leader scaffold company or team-wide OKRs down to a monthly, weekly or daily schedule. The goal is to help the leader avoid the mental gymnastics that come along with constant prioritization and rebalancing.
Accelerate User Adoption And Growth
For product-led growth (PLG) SaaS companies, AI could improve the user onboarding process and reduce the likelihood of customer churn by surfacing the right information for the right user at the right time. Research shows that 86% of customers will remain loyal when products provide onboarding and continuous education.
A user coming into an application for the first time should be greeted with a simple yet powerful experience, allowing them to put your product into action immediately and quickly begin to discern value. As their understanding of the product progresses, AI can gradually suggest additional, relevant functionalities and features for specific use cases. For companies with a freemium model, AI could suggest new features based on recommendations for specific users or even compare free users to paid peers to drive upgrades to paid subscriptions.
By establishing building blocks over time and growing with the user, companies could experience more healthy activations and retention—while helping their customers gain the most value from their applications.
From making products more accessible to improving the utility of your integrations ecosystem, AI has massive potential to transform the customer experience into one that delivers real impact. AI is here to become a companion for deeper innovation. Start by focusing on the applications that drive the most value for your customers. With that objective in mind, you’re headed on the right path toward generating the intended ROI from AI, all while creating a better product for your customers and prospects.

title: Council Post: Transforming Your Customer Experience With AI
text:
As Chief Availability Officer (CAO), Lou Senko leads Q2’s hosting team delivering an enhanced customer experience.
I was recently up late one night trying to fix my car with a fancy new tool that I couldn’t get to work properly and tried calling the company but their help desk was closed. So, I went on its website, where its support page bragged about a recent AI-empowered enhancement. Twenty-five search attempts later, I still didn’t have a solution to my problem. I did, however, find what looked like an internal company document comparing the features of my tool to a competitor’s tool, even describing the problem I was having. I logged onto the support system of the competitor and found its own document describing the problem and the workaround to fix it. I got my problem solved, but certainly not in the way the company that manufactured my tool intended.
My experience demonstrates the need to be smart when deploying AI tools for customer support because they have a way of accessing, synthesizing and sharing information that may have unintended consequences. That’s not to say that AI doesn’t have an exciting and vital role to play in improving the customer experience (CX).
Indeed, thanks to the widespread adoption of large language models (LLMs), we're far closer to realizing the ultimate goal of creating customers for life. It’s not just about one transaction or solving one problem. It’s about deepening customer relationships, creating partnerships and increasing customer lifetime value through intimate personalization.
It’s clear from recent polls that executives understand and want to leverage new AI tools for precisely this purpose. In a 2023 Gartner poll of 2,500 executive leaders, "38% of respondents consider customer experience/retention as their primary focus of generative AI investments...ahead of revenue growth (26%), cost optimization (17%) and business continuity (7%)."
One way companies have chosen to utilize the new tools is to give customers the power to solve their own problems without having to interact with a person. The theory is that customers prefer this model. (Of course, this offers better internal scaling, which helps the company’s bottom line.)
Not surprisingly, in a CMSWire survey from October 2023 of CX leaders, 60% expect AI to have a transformative or significant impact on their business. When asked where they expect AI and machine learning (ML) to have the greatest impact on their company's CX, "enabling customer self-service" led with 45%, followed by "gaining actionable customer insights" (44%), "improving customer retention" (34%), "helping us find customer experience problems faster" (32%) and "increasing customer lifetime value" (31%).
Many companies have already integrated and scaled internal use cases using AI to supercharge customer support teams, onboard new staff faster, close the gap between mediocre and stellar performers, and reduce the overall human effort. Because the tools are so effective in helping staff find solutions to problems, many companies want to turn these same tools outward and allow customers to interact with them directly. But it’s not that simple.
The tools are created and trained with a treasure trove of knowledge gleaned from playbooks, knowledge base articles and years of documented solutions within support cases. As customer service teams solve new problems, the solutions go into the training model, so the tools get progressively better at solving problems, ad infinitum.
However, because the systems are trained on knowledge from industry professionals, they rely heavily on technical jargon, and training customers to effectively query resources that use technical jargon is a nonstarter.
Enter LLMs. By incorporating them into the process, customers can ask their questions in natural language, which the LLM effectively translates to the jargon needed to locate the information to solve the problem. Unfortunately, this solution comes with a new set of challenges.
First, because the LLM returns a solution cobbled together from many different sources, it may lose its technical accuracy (e.g., the LLM finds the predictive next word from multiple unrelated documents that were never meant to be together). Because customers place a high degree of trust in the tool’s response, it’s important to ensure the answers are worthy of that trust.
Second, the answer may be so jargon-filled that the customer can’t do anything with it. Additionally, much of the knowledge needed to fix a technical problem is found in the private notes of customer service agents. Most support case systems allow companies to toggle what the customers are allowed to see and what's kept private, so they now need to allow customers to see those private notes to fix their problem, and those notes will need to be cleaned up for public consumption.
And then there’s the question of customer data security. Customer support teams need to be able to share fixes across their customer base in a way that doesn't unintentionally divulge private or proprietary information. Companies could allow the customer to search for answers but not return sensitive information to the person doing the search. It could also keep solutions for individual customers separate so one isn’t receiving private information about the other. Unfortunately, this separation of data could potentially reduce the effectiveness of the responses. If you tighten the scope to just the customers’ own data, they can’t leverage the larger collective wisdom to solve new problems.
These obstacles can be overcome, but they're complicated and require a larger investment of time and resources than many CX leaders plan for when implementing AI tools to enhance customer self-service. It’s also worth remembering that a vital part of creating customers for life is strengthening the personal connection, and this can only be done, well, in person. I can run through the self-checkout line myself or have a polite interaction with a person at the checkout counter and leave with a stronger, more pleasant memory connected to that business.
When customers have issues, we have opportunities to not just solve their problems but to deepen the customer relationship—one touch at a time.

title: The Digital Distiller: AI Transforms The Time Honored Art Of Whiskey Making
text:
In the world of whiskey production, tradition meets technology in a dramatic and transformative way. The ancient art, steeped in heritage and meticulous craft, is now embracing a new ally: artificial intelligence (AI). This fusion of age-old wisdom with cutting-edge AI is not just reinventing the process but is also redefining what whiskey can be.
The AI Revolution in Whiskey Production
The use of AI in whiskey production marks a bold step into the future while respecting and preserving the past. Distilleries, both venerable and new, harness AI to refine their craft, ensuring consistency, enhancing flavors, and even creating new blends that challenge the very notion of what whiskey can be. To begin with, the most significant impact of AI in whiskey production is in the creation of flavor profiles. Traditional whiskey making relies heavily on human expertise and intuition to develop flavors. However, AI introduces a new dimension to this process. For example, Mackmyra Whiskey, a Swedish distillery, made headlines by partnering with Microsoft and Fourkind to create the world’s first AI-developed whiskey. How dd they do this? The AI algorithm analyzed Mackmyra’s historical recipes, sales data, and customer preferences to generate a recipe that promised to be both popular and innovative.
Next, AI is also playing a critical role in ensuring consistency and quality in whiskey production. Distilleries like Macallan take advantage of AI-driven sensors and data analytics to monitor and control every stage of the whiskey-making process. From fermentation to aging, AI tools help in maintaining the optimal conditions needed for producing consistent, high-quality whiskey. Moreover, to maximize the value from this enhanced process, Macallan is also leveraging AI to train its staff in optimized distilling processes. Thus, Macallan is embracing the people, process, technology aspects of any good innovation.
Finally, sustainability is another key area where AI is making a significant impact. Distilleries tap into AI to optimize resource usage and reduce waste. Glenfiddich, for example, has started using AI to minimize energy consumption and manage by-products more efficiently, contributing to a more sustainable whiskey production process. Incredibly, this has led them to even fuel their trucks with whiskey waste.
The Art and Science of AI-Blended Whiskey
Mackmyra Whiskey’s AI-created spirit is a testament to the potential of AI in crafting unique flavor profiles. It represents a harmonious blend of human creativity and machine intelligence, producing a whiskey that is both innovative and deeply rooted in traditional craft. Moreover, AI monitoring is boosting quality enhancement. Distilleries like Jameson are exploring AI to monitor the aging process. AI systems equipped with sensors can analyze the chemical composition of the whiskey as it ages, ensuring each batch meets the high standards the brand is known for providing.
Perhaps, even more importantly, is the “holy grail” in the whiskey industry: customized whiskey. This concept goes beyond flavor profiles, which is about matching making. Imagine that a batch of whiskey is specifically tailored for the tastebuds of a specific customer. This is not far from becoming a mainstream reality. Thanks to AI, whiskey producers have the ability to manage whiskey making at a microscale with additional little cost, enabling a whole new level of premium services within the industry. This approach will revolutionize how consumers interact with whiskey brands, offering a deeply personal and unique experience.
Embracing the Digital Distillation Era
As we stand on the brink of this new era in whiskey production, the role of AI is both exhilarating and profound. The combination of AI with traditional distilling methods is not just about creating better whiskey; it's about reimagining the entire whiskey experience. For whiskey enthusiasts, distillers, and innovators, AI invites us to be part of a journey that respects tradition while boldly embracing the future. For whiskey producers, AI unlocks product efficiencies, a new set of blends, and level of precision flavor that distillers only dreamed about.
Let’s raise a glass to this exciting journey, where the age-old art of whiskey making meets the transformative power of AI. Together, we are not just witnessing the evolution of whiskey; we are part of it. The future of whiskey is here, and it's smarter, more sustainable, and more personalized than ever before. Let’s savor the taste of innovation and tradition, blended beautifully by the digital distiller.

title: Qualcomm Becomes Major Player In the AI PC Race
text:
For at least a decade now, Qualcomm has been pushing the concept of the "connected PC." Their Snapdragon chip is at the heart of billions of smartphones, and to broaden their reach, they started targeting PCs, using their chips to give PCs any-time, anywhere connectivity.
At one of their first analysts events in Maui, Hawaii, towards the end of the last decade, they shared their vision for a new high-powered, low-energy chip that could run a special version of Windows adapted for their ARM-based processors and be used in traditional PCs. The design included their modem chip. They called it the Always-On PC program and pushed software and hardware vendors to help them bring their ARM-based Snapdragon to the PC world.
Although the connected PC program never took off, Qualcomm now believes that a new version of its Snapdragon processors can deliver a powerful processor for PCs that can compete with similar ones from Intel and AMD in the race to provide next-generation AI-based PCs. Their new AI PC processor is called the Snapdragon X Elite, and the Qualcomm tagline is "the AI super-charged platform to revolutionize the PC."
This move represents a significant expansion of Qualcomm's technological prowess, aiming to redefine the PC experience by integrating advanced artificial intelligence capabilities. By leveraging its expertise in power-efficient, high-performance mobile processors, Qualcomm intends to bring to the PC market what it has perfected for smartphones: seamless connectivity, extended battery life, and now, cutting-edge AI functionalities.
This strategic shift is not just about enhancing computational power or efficiency; it's about reimagining what PCs can do with AI at their core. This vision is shared by Intel, AMD, Microsoft, and others who are creating a new generation of PCs that are capable of delivering AI functionalities on the PC itself.
Indeed, last fall, Intel held a major event to launch its AI PC program, with Microsft helping to lead the transition from standard PCs to this new era of AI PCs. But at the time, Intel's push was for chips made only by Intel and AMD based on Intel core architecture.
But Qualcomm has been working on advanced AI-focused Snapdragon processors and has now become a serious alternative to AI PCs based on chips using Intel architecture. Qualcomm has shown media and analysts the capabilities of the Snapdragon X Elite and demonstrated how this chip can compete with processors from Intel and AMD but has better battery life. These chipsets leverage Qualcomm's expertise in mobile technology to deliver always-on connectivity and extended battery life, which is essential for today's mobile workforce.
The key drawback is that Windows has to run mostly in emulation mode on ARM-based systems. However, Microsoft has worked with Qualcomm on a native version of Windows for this platform and made native apps. This week, Google announced they would make a native version of their Chrome browser that works with the Snapdragon Elite X processor. Given the capabilities of this new Qualcomm chip, I suspect we will begin to see more dedicated apps written natively to support Qualcomm's AI PC effort.
Given the power of Intel and AMD in the traditional PC market, Qualcomm is looked on by many as a dark horse in the AI PC race. But, Qualcomm has demonstrated to media and analysts that the Snapdragon X Elite poses a strong challenge to Intel and AMD. It should be recognized as a major player in the effort to establish the AI PC as a prominent technology in the PC market within the next three years.
Disclosure: Qualcomm subscribes to Creative Strategies research reports along with many high tech companies around the world.

text:
